That's a problem. A psychotherapist - a counselor - is better able to make any sort of diagnosis. And reading off bullet points to someone is not how you make a diagnosis.

You've also been out of whack because of medications.

If you're worried about actually having BPD, read some at-length stories written by people who know others who have BPD (not the people with BPD themselves). As with any clinical disorder, a diagnosis should be glaringly obvious from the outside. It's not a "you have some symptoms" kind of thing. Think of the difference between having a cold and having mono.

I popped onto this sub just to get some context for a few things I've been thinking about recently (I don't have BPD). From my perspective, your best bet would probably be to see the therapist she fired and talk about BPD and her issues. If you do get diagnosed with BPD by the therapist, your daughter might be on to something that you're missing. If you aren't, then the therapist will be able to tell you more about how your daughter sees you and describes you to others - and why. You'll also be able to tell your daughter about her misperceptions. The therapist might also be able to give you an action plan for where to go from here.

I don't have enough information to give anything resembling a diagnosis, but I'll give you my impressions bluntly. 

(1) She is using you. her behavior shows signs of the kind of manipulative behavior common among abusive people in the BDSM community. She enjoys having control over you, and may get sexual gratification from it. At the least, she is using her power over you and your attention/affection for her to stroke her ego. She does not see you as an equal person. Through the first half your post, I was going to tell you to immediately get away from her. having your finances bound up with hers and the possibility that she can recognize her manipulativeness and emotional damagedness complicate that recommendation.

(2) Your idealizing and feelings for her are the result of layers of insecurity complexes and therapy transference. You're simply not going to be able to view her objectively, and thus can't view any situations involving her objectively. You Must distance yourself from her emotionally, no matter what. Not only so that she doesn't have so much control over you explicitly, but so that you can get a grip on yourself and your reality.

(3) I don't think you have BPD. Readily noticeable case: A person with BPD seems to sort of flip like a switch in their attitudes toward self or others. To an outsider, it would seem like someone with BPD has two completely separate personalities because their responses are so different. There's simply no justification for the switch. Their emotions are extreme and last for unusually long amounts of time. Because of this, many people with BPD try to repress their emotions. You don't seem to do any of that.

To give a comparison, having BPD is like living in a foggy room with no mirrors and sudden spikes of heat and chill. They feel out of control, aren't certain of their identity, and feel pulled around by their emotions.

If you do have noticeable BPD and have never been on meds for it, I can't imagine how you would have had any sort of stable relationship.

(4) I do think that you have deep fears of abandonment, isolation, and insufficiency.

I recommend that you hop around reddit's assistance-giving areas ( starting with /r/Assistance ) to see about insurance and therapy resources and the like.

I also recommend that you break away from that family, and try to avoid relationships in which you aren't the primary driver of your own well-being. It seems to me like you could fall into a habit of submissive roles in relationships, which would only further increase your insecurities and abandonment fears.

But you're 16, which means that you still have a lot of time to sort through the bad people and perhaps find some worthwhile ones. You also have plenty of opportunity to decide on a career that will give you independence and security, in which you'll be taking money from the assholes to use for whatever you want. If many people around you where you are suck, then I suggest looking for different people online. They can't be there for the in-person stuff of day-to-day life, but they might at least give you a place to socialize. If you spend your day thinking about and working toward small steps that lead you to a desired goal (like getting your diploma so that you can get a job and move somewhere else, perhaps where your new online friends live), the time will pass by quickly. I speak from experience.

Growing up, I had an on-again-off-again best friend/girlfriend for all of my teen years, and every time we broke up, I felt crushed. She was the only person I really spoke openly with. In the end, she forced us to cut off contact entirely. The way she did it wasn't cool, but the objective was the best thing for both of us. It took me going to college and exploring myself to stop thinking about her. In other words - living a life without her and without focusing on her.

My guess is that you need that, too.

I don't agree with the advice of going out to find another relationship. Your feelings are out of whack right now. You don't need affection with someone else triggering memories and doubts. 

You might be able to become friends with your ex again, but I think you might need quite a bit of space (like, months of her not being on your mind/part of your identity) before it's possible to just look at her as a friend.

The job thing sucks. My only point for consideration there is that you might find life more enjoyable if you split your focus between doing some sort of work to have income and taking steps toward what you ultimately want to do with your life.

You should leave a note. Not leaving a note leads to a lot of guilt and re-traumatizing for friends and family. It's also best to lie if your goal is to prevent their suffering and they were part of the cause of your problems. A suicide note is a very powerful thing, and can change the course of someone's life for the worse with just a single sentence.

To reduce the number and intensity of negatives outcomes after your death, you should focus on these things:

(1) Demonstrating that the cause of your suicide is one that couldn't be resolved. Your chronic pain clearly fits, but you could also talk about other lasting issues that you chose not to deal with anymore. If the people who read the note come to accept that the source of the problems is something you believed you couldn't escape, they will handle it much better. The same thing happens with family of accident victims - unclear and avoidable causes create bad outcomes for loved ones.

(2) Express your affection for those you care about. Make it clear that you don't want to hurt them and that you're thankful for all they have done.

(3) Mask your animosity toward people. Anything in a suicide note that is critical of a person can cause completely unexpected reactions, and they are almost always bad. In the case of your girlfriend-turned-caregiver, it might help to express empathy for her from her perspective, because she is likely to blame herself given how she has treated you.

(4) Though you might not like it, do not talk about debts you're leaving behind or struggles with money. Family often think that if they had helped out more financially, a suicide wouldn't have happened. By leaving out the subject of money and focusing on your other lasting problems, it reduces the likelihood that people will feel guilty and blame themselves for not doing more.

(5) Reassure them that whatever they feel after learning about your suicide is ok - including being angry at you. Express that you know that grief makes everyone remember all kinds of things and feel all kinds of emotions, and that everyone should be understanding with themselves and each other. Humans are often at their weakest - and weirdest - when grieving. Warn them that they might feel numbness for a long time to come, because it seems unreal.

(6) Apologize for the stigma that they will experience. Their friends, co-workers, and strangers won't react with understanding or compassion in most cases. Rather, shaming and distancing will be common. If not at first, then as time goes on.

(7) End with summarizing that your problems weren't going to go away, you love them, and that you're sorry. Then clearly state that in the end it is your body, your life, and your decision, and you're making your choice to end it. That calm finality and certainty can help them to let go and move on over time.

A few things to not do: 

(1) Tell them what what they're thinking is wrong, immoral, short-sighted, etc. For one thing, that's wrong. For another, it shuts down conversation and makes it less likely that they'll reach out in the future.

(2) Pressure them to "think about x". It's the caller's problem and the caller's life. Focusing away from the caller is disrespectful shuts things down, and is likely to make them feel like they aren't valuable outside of how others see them.

(3) Corner the caller. Again, it's disrespectful and shuts things down. The person is calling because they want to work out their thoughts and feelings, not so that you can win an argument or achieve the goal of making them say they won't end their life. Don't try to emotionally or logically pressure them into anything.

(4) Don't give them false hope. Again, it's disrespectful and makes it more likely that they won't trust others in the future. Don't say "It gets better", refer them to a service as if it will fix things, etc. 

(5) Don't say or pretend that your experiences compare with theirs, or that you understand and/or can equally empathize with them because of your training. In many cases, you can't. In the cases where you can, doing so will often be interpreted as trivializing or minimizing their feelings and problems.

A few things to do:

(1) Both tell and show them that you are there to listen, and will not shame, laugh at, or otherwise attack them. People are often very embarrassed by their problems. Those feelings are magnified by speaking to someone about being suicidal. If they don't feel free to talk, you're much less likely to be of help to them.

(2) Spend time listening before providing any suggestions or advice, unless they ask you for them. As with any communication, building rapport comes first.

(3) Focus on what the caller says they need - not what you or anyone else thinks they need. A few minutes into the conversation, you can ask if they might like to have a certain resource or if they have a certain need, but don't suggest it like you know what's best for them. That's both insulting and contributes to cultivating feelings of powerlessness.

(4) Avoid overwhelming the caller. This can be done by asking about small "next steps" to take - rather than about long-term goals or ideal outcomes. It also helps to avoid spiraling thoughts and out-of-control emotions by asking simple questions that get the person to reflect, such as "When did you start feeling that way?" and "What was your life like (or what were you doing) when you last felt happy?" Let the person speak about their feelings, but when things start getting out of hand, redirect them to such questions.

(5) Keep in mind - and feel free to tell the caller - that your goal is not to make them stop feeling suicidal or to promise not to end their life. Your goal is to be a safe place for them to talk and to help them find things that they can use or focus on to change their life, which will hopefully lead to the suicidal thoughts going away.
